source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What kind of system of government does the UK have?

options.text: A parliamentary democracy with the monarch as head of state

explanation_simple: The UK is a parliamentary democracy with the monarch as head of state.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? The British constitution is written down in a single document.
explanation_simple: The British constitution is not written down in any single document, so it is sometimes described as 'unwritten'.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: The UK has a constitutional monarchy. What does this mean?

options.text: The monarch makes all the laws
The monarch is elected every five years
The monarch does not rule the country but appoints the government, which people choose in elections
The monarch leads the largest political party

explanation_simple: In a constitutional monarchy the monarch does not rule the country. The government is chosen in democratic elections.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Who is the head of the Commonwealth?

options.text: The Speaker of the House of Commons
The Secretary-General of the United Nations

explanation_simple: The monarch is head of state of the UK and head of the Commonwealth.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which TWO of these are key institutions of the British constitution?

options.text: The Bank of England's board of shareholders

explanation_simple: Key institutions include the monarchy, Parliament, the Prime Minister and cabinet, the judiciary, the police, the civil service and local government.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which of these statements is correct?

options.text: Parliament is made up of the House of Commons and the Senate.
Parliament is made up of the House of Commons and the House of Lords.

explanation_simple: The UK Parliament has two houses: the elected House of Commons and the House of Lords, whose members are not elected.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? The House of Commons can overrule the House of Lords.
explanation_simple: The House of Commons is regarded as the more important chamber. The Lords can suggest changes to laws, and the Commons can overrule them.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which TWO kinds of people can sit in the House of Lords?

options.text: Bishops of the Church of England
Life peers appointed by the monarch
Members elected at a general election

explanation_simple: Members of the House of Lords are not elected. They include life peers, some hereditary peers and senior bishops of the Church of England.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Who appoints life peers to the House of Lords?

options.text: The monarch, on the advice of the Prime Minister
The Speaker of the House of Commons

explanation_simple: Life peers are appointed by the monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister. They do not pass their title on.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What is the role of the Speaker in the House of Commons?

options.text: To chair debates and keep order, staying politically neutral

explanation_simple: The Speaker chairs debates in the House of Commons and keeps order. The Speaker is neutral and is chosen by other MPs in a secret ballot.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? The Speaker of the House of Commons is chosen by other MPs in a secret ballot.
explanation_simple: MPs elect the Speaker in a secret ballot.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What does a Member of Parliament (MP) represent?

options.text: Only the people who voted for them
A whole region of the UK
Only members of their own party

explanation_simple: Each MP represents everyone in their constituency, which is a local area.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Number of constituencies. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: How many parliamentary constituencies is the UK divided into?
explanation_simple: The UK is divided into 650 parliamentary constituencies, each electing one MP.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What happens if an MP dies or resigns?

options.text: The seat stays empty until the next general election
The Prime Minister chooses a replacement
A by-election is held in their constituency

explanation_simple: If an MP dies or resigns there is a by-election, an election in that constituency only.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: How are MPs elected to the House of Commons?

options.text: By proportional representation across the whole UK
By a 'first past the post' system: the candidate with the most votes wins

explanation_simple: MPs are elected through a 'first past the post' system. The candidate who gets the most votes in a constituency is elected.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What do party 'whips' do in Parliament?

options.text: Ensure discipline and that MPs attend to vote

explanation_simple: Whips are a small group of MPs appointed by their party leaders to ensure discipline and attendance at votes.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What is the official home of the Prime Minister in London?
explanation_simple: The Prime Minister's official home is 10 Downing Street. There is also a country house outside London called Chequers.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What is the name of the Prime Minister's country house outside London?
explanation_simple: Chequers is the Prime Minister's country house outside London.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Who usually becomes Prime Minister?

options.text: The Speaker of the House of Commons
The leader of the party that wins the most seats in a general election
The person chosen by the House of Lords
The oldest MP in the House of Commons

explanation_simple: The Prime Minister is the leader of the political party in power, usually the party with the most MPs.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: 'About 20' figure. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Who appoints the members of the cabinet?
explanation_simple: The Prime Minister appoints about 20 senior MPs to the cabinet, which meets weekly to make decisions on government policy.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which cabinet minister is responsible for the economy?
explanation_simple: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the economy.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which cabinet minister is responsible for crime, policing and immigration?
explanation_simple: The Home Secretary is responsible for crime, policing and immigration.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which cabinet minister manages the UK's relationship with other countries?
explanation_simple: The Foreign Secretary manages relationships with foreign countries.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which party forms the official opposition?

options.text: The largest party in the House of Lords
The smallest party in the House of Commons
Any party chosen by the Speaker
The second-largest party in the House of Commons

explanation_simple: The second-largest party in the House of Commons is the opposition. Its leader is the Leader of the Opposition.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? The Leader of the Opposition appoints senior opposition MPs to a 'shadow cabinet'.
explanation_simple: The Leader of the Opposition leads a shadow cabinet whose members each follow a government department.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: How often does Prime Minister's Questions take place while Parliament is sitting?
explanation_simple: Prime Minister's Questions takes place every week while Parliament is sitting; the Leader of the Opposition usually asks questions.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? Civil servants are chosen by the political party in power and must support it.
explanation_simple: Civil servants carry out government policy but are politically neutral. They are not political appointees.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Year 1999. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: In which city does the Scottish Parliament sit?
explanation_simple: The Scottish Parliament sits in Edinburgh, at Holyrood. It was formed in 1999.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: The body is now called the Senedd; keep the handbook's name in the explanation. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Where does the devolved parliament (assembly) for Wales sit?
explanation_simple: The National Assembly for Wales sits in Cardiff. It was established in 1999.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Confirm examples of devolved and reserved matters. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which TWO of these can the Scottish Parliament make laws on?
explanation_simple: The Scottish Parliament can pass laws on matters not reserved to the UK Parliament, such as education and health. Defence and foreign affairs remain with the UK Parliament.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Year 1998. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? The Northern Ireland Assembly was set up after the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement of 1998.
explanation_simple: The Northern Ireland Assembly was established soon after the Belfast Agreement in 1998.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Confirm the handbook's wording on broadcasters' balance. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? Newspapers in the UK are free to give their own political opinions.
explanation_simple: The UK has a free press. Newspapers are often biased towards a party, but radio and TV coverage of political parties must be balanced.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which TWO groups of adults resident in the UK can vote in all public elections?

options.text: Citizens of any country who have lived in the UK for one year

explanation_simple: British citizens and citizens of the Commonwealth and the Irish Republic who are resident in the UK can vote in all public elections.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What must you do before you can vote?

options.text: Pass a test about the candidates
Have your name on the electoral register

explanation_simple: To vote in an election you must have your name on the electoral register.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Hours. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: On election day, what are the usual opening hours of polling stations?
explanation_simple: Polling stations are usually open from 7 am to 10 pm on election day.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Keep 'according to the handbook': voting ages are changing in some UK elections. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: According to the handbook, what is the minimum age for voting in UK Parliament elections?
explanation_simple: The handbook gives 18 as the voting age for UK Parliament elections.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: How often must a general election be held in the UK?
explanation_simple: MPs are elected at a general election, which is held at least every five years.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? Voting in UK elections is done by secret ballot.
explanation_simple: Elections are held by secret ballot, and you can also apply to vote by post.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What is the minimum age to stand for public office, such as an MP?
explanation_simple: Most citizens of the UK, the Irish Republic or the Commonwealth aged 18 or over can stand for public office.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Many MPs hold local sessions where constituents can meet them. What are these called?
explanation_simple: Many MPs hold regular local 'surgeries' where constituents can go to see them in person.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What is the Commonwealth?

options.text: A military alliance led by the USA
A group of countries that must follow UK law
A voluntary association of countries, most of which were once part of the British Empire
An organisation of European countries only

explanation_simple: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of countries. Most were once part of the British Empire. Members work together towards shared goals.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? The UK is one of five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.
explanation_simple: The UK is part of the United Nations and is one of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What is NATO?

options.text: A trade agreement between European countries
A group of countries that have agreed to help each other if they are attacked

explanation_simple: NATO is a group of European and North American countries that have agreed to help each other if they come under attack.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which important agreement did the Council of Europe create?

options.text: The European Convention on Human Rights

explanation_simple: The Council of Europe created the European Convention on Human Rights. It is separate from the European Union.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which of these statements is correct?

options.text: Civil law is used to settle disputes between individuals or groups.
Civil law is used to punish people who commit serious crimes such as theft.

explanation_simple: Criminal law deals with crimes, which are investigated by the police. Civil law settles disputes, for example about housing or employment.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which TWO of these are examples of civil law disputes?

options.text: An argument about faulty goods bought from a shop
A disagreement between a landlord and tenant

explanation_simple: Civil law covers disputes such as housing, employment and consumer rights. Carrying a weapon and burglary are crimes.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? Selling tobacco to anyone under 18 is a criminal offence.
explanation_simple: It is a criminal offence to sell tobacco products to anyone under 18.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which TWO of these are duties of the police?

options.text: Deciding the sentence for a crime

explanation_simple: The police protect life and property, prevent disturbances (keep the peace), and prevent and detect crime. Courts decide sentences and Parliament makes laws.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What does a Police Community Support Officer (PCSO) do?

options.text: Patrols the streets, works with the public and supports police officers

explanation_simple: PCSOs patrol the streets, work with the public and support police officers at crime scenes and major events.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Year 2012. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Since 2012, who sets local police priorities in England and Wales?
explanation_simple: Since November 2012, people in England and Wales have elected Police and Crime Commissioners, who set local police priorities.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, most minor criminal cases are dealt with in which court?
explanation_simple: Most minor criminal cases are heard in a Magistrates' Court. In Scotland they go to a Justice of the Peace Court.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? Magistrates in England and Wales are usually unpaid volunteers without legal qualifications.
explanation_simple: Magistrates and Justices of the Peace are members of the local community. They are usually unpaid and do not need legal qualifications.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: How many members are on a jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
explanation_simple: Juries in England, Wales and Northern Ireland have 12 members. In Scotland a jury has 15 members.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: How many members are on a jury in Scotland?
explanation_simple: Scottish juries have 15 members; juries elsewhere in the UK have 12.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Young people aged 10 to 17 accused of a crime are usually tried in which court?
explanation_simple: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, people aged 10 to 17 accused of a crime are tried in a Youth Court, before up to three specially trained magistrates or a District Judge.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, serious criminal offences are tried where?

options.text: In a Crown Court, in front of a judge and jury

explanation_simple: Serious offences are tried in front of a judge and a jury in a Crown Court. In Scotland they are tried in a Sheriff Court or the High Court.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Do not quote money limits; they have changed since 2013. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What is the small claims procedure?

options.text: A way of appealing against a parking fine
A procedure for claiming welfare benefits
An informal way of settling disputes involving smaller amounts of money, without a lawyer
A court for crimes involving theft

explanation_simple: The small claims procedure helps people settle disputes over smaller amounts of money without a lawyer, at an informal hearing.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Organisation name as printed in the handbook. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Where can you get free advice about legal problems, debt or housing?
explanation_simple: Citizens Advice gives free, confidential advice on many problems, including legal matters, debt and housing.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? In the UK, a man who forces his wife to have sex can be charged with rape.
explanation_simple: Domestic violence is a serious crime. Anyone who is violent towards their partner, including forcing them to have sex, can be prosecuted.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? Female genital mutilation (FGM) is illegal in the UK.
explanation_simple: FGM is a crime in the UK, and it is also a crime to take a girl abroad for FGM.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? A marriage in which one person does not consent is legal in the UK if the families agree.
explanation_simple: Forced marriage, where one or both people do not consent, is a crime. Arranged marriages, where both agree, are different.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which Act brought the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law?

options.text: The Representation of the People Act 1918

explanation_simple: The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which TWO of these rights are protected by the European Convention on Human Rights?

options.text: Freedom of thought, conscience and religion
The right to a job of your choice
The right to a fair trial

explanation_simple: Rights protected include the right to life, prohibition of torture, the right to liberty and a fair trial, freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and freedom of expression.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? In the UK it is against the law to treat someone unfairly at work because of their sex, race or disability.
explanation_simple: UK laws ensure people are not treated unfairly because of characteristics such as age, disability, sex, race, religion or sexual orientation.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What is the minimum age to drive a car in the UK?
explanation_simple: You must be at least 17 years old to drive a car or motorcycle, and you must have a driving licence.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Cars over three years old must pass which yearly test?
explanation_simple: If your vehicle is over three years old, you must take it for a Ministry of Transport (MOT) test every year.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? It is a criminal offence to drive a car without insurance.
explanation_simple: Drivers must have valid motor insurance. Driving without it is a serious criminal offence.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Confirm the handbook's wording. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Which organisation collects income tax in the UK?

options.text: The Department for Work and Pensions

explanation_simple: Income tax is collected by HM Revenue & Customs. Many people have it taken from their pay through PAYE.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: National Insurance contributions are used to pay for what?

options.text: State benefits and services such as the state pension and the NHS

explanation_simple: National Insurance contributions pay for state benefits and services, such as the state retirement pension and the National Health Service.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Confirm whether the handbook covers council tax in this chapter. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What is council tax used for?
explanation_simple: Council tax is a local tax that helps pay for local services such as rubbish collection and schools.

source.reviewer_note: CHECK FIRST: Age range; it has changed since 2013. Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Who can be asked to do jury service?

options.text: Anyone on the electoral register aged 18 to 70

explanation_simple: Anyone on the electoral register aged 18 to 70 can be asked to serve on a jury.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? Volunteering is a good way to support your community and meet new people.
explanation_simple: Volunteering helps others, builds your community and can give you useful experience.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: What can people in the UK donate to help save lives in hospitals?
explanation_simple: Donated blood is used in hospitals to help people with injuries and illnesses. Many people also register as organ donors.

source.reviewer_note: Confirm the section heading wording in the handbook

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? Recycling as much as possible is one way of looking after the environment.
explanation_simple: Looking after the environment includes recycling, not dropping litter and using public transport, walking or cycling.
